questions.q: Define 'dignity of labour' as given in the NCERT textbook and give one example from the text illustrating it.
questions.a: Dignity of labour means taking pride in whatever work one does, regardless of its nature or status; the textbook illustrates this with Mahatma Gandhi doing sweeping, scavenging, and cleaning in his ashram and cleaning his own toilet to demonstrate that no work is inferior or menial. A wrong answer (e.g., "dignity of labour means only respecting high-status jobs") reveals the student confuses social prestige with intrinsic worth of work, missing the textbook's emphasis that all honest work deserves equal respect.

questions.q: Explain the difference between 'values' and 'ethics' in a professional context using the textbook's definitions. Why does the textbook say ethics are 'a formal system or set of rules explicitly adopted by a group'?
questions.a: Values are personal beliefs, preferences, or assumptions about what is desirable or good (e.g., integrity, service); ethics are formal, codified rules explicitly adopted by a professional group (e.g., medical ethics, professional ethics) that govern conduct. The textbook calls ethics a 'formal system' because they are written, agreed upon, and enforceable within a profession, unlike values which are internal and subjective. A wrong answer (e.g., "values and ethics are the same thing") shows the student cannot distinguish internal moral compass from external professional standards — a critical gap for board exam questions on professional conduct.

questions.q: A junior dietitian in a hospital observes that the senior dietitian consistently alters patient meal plans to use cheaper, lower-quality ingredients to cut costs, without informing patients or doctors. The junior fears retaliation if they report it. Using the six core values from the textbook, identify which values are violated and propose an ethically defensible first step the junior should take.
questions.a: Violated values: (1) Integrity — dishonesty in altering plans; (2) Dignity and worth of persons — patients' right to proper nutrition disregarded; (3) Social justice — unfair cost-cutting at expense of vulnerable patients; (4) Service — primary duty to patient well-being compromised. First step: Document observations factually and raise concern privately with the senior dietitian, citing patient safety and professional ethics, before escalating. This applies the textbook's emphasis on ethical conduct reducing waste and increasing morale. A wrong answer (e.g., "stay silent to keep the job") reveals the student prioritises self-preservation over professional ethics, missing that the textbook states 'being ethical at all times earns respect of colleagues'.

questions.q: Compare the textbook's view of 'work as a calling' with 'work as a job' and 'work as a career'. How does the concept of dignity of labour bridge these three perspectives?
questions.a: Work as a job: done for income, satisfaction from pay. Work as a career: done for advancement, satisfaction from progress. Work as a calling: done for inner fulfilment, satisfaction from the work itself. Dignity of labour bridges them by asserting that ALL three — whether breaking rocks for wages, carving a statue for mastery, or serving a higher purpose — deserve equal respect because each involves honest human effort contributing to society. The textbook's three stone-breakers illustrate this: the first has a job, second a livelihood, third a calling/career, yet all perform labour. A wrong answer (e.g., "only work as a calling has dignity") shows the student imposes a hierarchy the textbook explicitly rejects, confusing personal fulfilment with intrinsic worth of labour.

questions.q: Critique this statement using the textbook: "Professional ethics only apply to high-status professions like doctors and lawyers; a domestic worker or factory labourer doesn't need professional ethics, just honesty."
questions.a: The statement is false. The textbook states: "In all work settings, generic norms of ethics and dignity are applicable" and "Every human being is infinitely worthy; however, in modern times wealth is being given more importance. Whatever the type of work done, or the position held, or financial status, every person deserves respect." The Universal Declaration of Human Rights cited in the text applies to all workers. Domestic workers and factory labourers are explicitly mentioned as 'special groups' whose presence has 'implications for quality of life and society'. A wrong answer (e.g., agreeing with the statement) reveals the student equates professional ethics with formal codes of licensed professions, missing the textbook's universalist stance that ethics are generic norms for ALL work.

questions.q: Design a 5-point 'Ethical Workplace Charter' for a small home-based catering business employing 3 women from a low-income neighbourhood. Base each point on one of the six core values from the textbook, and explain how it protects both the employer's and employees' dignity.
questions.a: Sample charter: (1) Integrity — Transparent pricing and ingredient sourcing; protects employer's reputation and employees' pride in honest work. (2) Dignity and worth of persons — Fair wages, safe kitchen, no exploitation; protects employees' human dignity and employer's moral standing. (3) Service — Nutritious, hygienic meals for clients; fulfills professional duty and builds trust. (4) Human relationships — Weekly feedback circle, grievance redressal; nurtures mutual respect. (5) Social justice — Skill training for employees to advance; addresses power imbalance. Competence (6th value) is embedded in training. A poor answer (e.g., generic rules like "be on time") shows the student cannot translate abstract values into contextualised ethical practices — a key board exam skill.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Work ethics refers to the set of moral principles and values that guide professional conduct, including integrity, accountability, diligence, and respect for the dignity of all labour; ______ is the consistent demonstration of these ethics through competence, reliability, ethical decision-making, and commitment to quality in one's work role, irrespective of the job's status or remuneration.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are interning at a design firm and notice a senior ______ presenting your original concept as their own to the client.
What is Work ethics? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Work ethics refers to the set of moral principles and values that guide professional conduct, including integrity, accountability, diligence, and respect for the dignity of all labour; professionalism is the consistent demonstration of these ethics through competence, reliability, ethical decision-making, and commitment to quality in.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Work ethics?
questions.a: Students often believe 'professionalism' means only external behaviours — dressing formally, speaking politely, meeting deadlines — and that 'ethics' are relevant only in crises (e.g., whistleblowing).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can analyse a workplace scenario to identify ethical dilemmas, apply the six core values (service, social justice, dignity and worth of persons, human relationships, integrity, competence) to resolve them, and justify their resolution using the concept of dignity of labour and professional ethics.
